name: Assistive Technology and Communication
title: Assistive Technology and Communication
answer: Assistive technology can change a student's education when the right tool is matched to the right student. AI can help school teams search vendor catalogs and compare options, but the assistive technology specialist, the family, and the student make the final choice. The idea matters because access and inclusion depend on trained people, not just devices.

sections.body: This idea is about choosing and using assistive technology and communication tools so students with disabilities can access learning and express themselves. It solves the problem of devices that are purchased but not matched to a student's needs or supported by trained staff. The text describes tools for communication, math, and braille, including symbol based communication apps, sound based graph exploration, and braille translation. It also names training as the barrier that research reports most often. The core task is not simply buying technology but building the adult and student skills that make the technology useful.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, teams begin by matching a tool to a specific student, with AI helping to search vendor catalogs and compare options. For students who cannot rely on speech, augmentative and alternative communication devices such as Proloquo2Go use symbols and word prediction to help build messages, and AI powered word prediction can speed communication. For math and braille, Desmos accessibility features let students who are blind explore graphs through sound, and braille translation software can convert materials for students who read braille. The text does not give grade bands for these practices, so the same principles apply across ages. Training should reach every adult who works with the student and the student too, so the student can use the tools independently.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites a review of 31 studies by Fernandez-Batanero in 2022, which found that assistive technology increases inclusion and access for students with disabilities. That review also found that the main barriers are teacher training, information, and accessibility. The text states that Proloquo2Go costs about $250 on the App Store. It also states that Desmos has accessibility features that let students who are blind explore graphs through sound, and that braille translation software can convert materials for students who read braille. The text does not give a separate evidence label beyond this review, and it says training is the barrier the research names most often, with devices sitting in drawers when a district buys assistive technology without teacher training.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text: AI can help search catalogs and compare options, but it does not choose the tool. The assistive technology specialist, the family, and the student make the choice. For communication devices, the vocabulary, symbols, and settings must be chosen with the speech pathologist and family so the device reflects the student's own voice. For braille, a teacher of the visually impaired should check the output. Training is also a guardrail, because budgets should include training for every adult who works with the student and for the student, so devices do not sit unused.
